Rolling Release Vs. Fixed Release Distros; Which Linux Distributions Are Better?

Just to add my two cents I usually go with fixed release because I have no use for bleeding edge software usually and If I do want that, I can usually get it anyway through unofficial but reasonably safe sources. The only thing I want is timely security updates and most distros provide that on fixed release cycles. Having looked into snap packages and flatpacks, it seems if these take off it will mean self-contained software releases with dependencies packed in so that will make it even easier.

Rolling release. I'm a linux gamer and I need access to the latest unix drivers being released by Nvidia. Linux Mint did not give me that, and yes, while I could have downloaded the driver and installed it manually, I probably would have end up breaking something and I doubt the Linux Mint community would have supported me in resolving said breakage.

With rolling, I get the latest software, but crucially, support for that latest software.
Would it be fair to say rolling releases have vastly improved stability in the last few years and less software breakages from what they used to be?

I can't speak for how things used to be, but from my experience with a rolling distro this last year, I can say things can and will still break from time to time.

We've had the annoying transition to GTK 3.20, which broke many themes. The metamodes bug, introduced by Nvidia in one of their driver releases. And now we are going through the painful XOrg 1.18 move, which is playing havoc with AMD users running on older cards.

The Manjaro team attempt to resolve such issues before releasing updates to stable, but it is impossible to take the time to anticipate everything and still call themselves a rolling distro, and then sometimes, like with AMD Catalyst and XOrg, there really is little they can do to stop that causing issues.

That said, I have learned more about Linux and how the operating system functions by using a rolling distro, than I ever did while running Mint. Most fixes are simple, and some problems avoidable, if one reads the Unstable and Testing branch update threads to see what issues were encountered.

Meh... I know you don't get the latest drivers from the standard repos in Ubuntu/Mint, but there are repos out there now that cater to this, so the fix is really as simple as one add-apt-repository command. This really isn't the big gripe that it used to be.

Honestly, as a gamer, I'm more concerned with getting a kernel major revision change that I didn't notice coming in, and having all of my shit broken for the next several hours as I install dependencies and get everything back into a functional state.

Rolling, it is pretty great to install once and just stay up to date as you go. On something like Gentoo the default stable branch is actually really stable too, so you can have stability AND rolling release
